tip: 'Vouloir dire' literally reads 'to want to say', but together it just means 'to mean': 'qu'est-ce que ça veut dire' = what does that mean?
In everyday French, 'on' means 'we': 'où est-ce qu'on se retrouve' = where do we meet? It takes a singular verb even though it means us.
A day 'passes itself' in French: comment s'est passée ta journée. Se passer means to happen, and it takes être in the past.

target: Je ne mange jamais de viande.
tip: 'Ne...jamais de' = never any. Same rule: un/une/du/de la become 'de' in negative: Je ne bois jamais de café.

target: Parlez plus lentement, s'il vous plaît.
tip: French builds adverbs much like English '-ly', by adding '-ment': lent (slow) becomes 'lentement' (slowly). So 'plus lentement' = more slowly.
French can't strand a preposition at the end: it's 'pour qui est ce cadeau', literally 'for whom is this gift', never a dangling 'for'.
Languages take a definite article in French: you don't learn 'French', you learn 'le français' – hence 'apprends le français'.

target: Il y a trop de bruit.
tip: 'Il y a' covers both 'there is' and 'there are' – it never changes for number: 'il y a trop de bruit', il y a trois livres.

target: Le bureau du directeur est grand.
tip: 'Du' = de + le (contraction). 'Des' = de + les. These contractions are mandatory: le livre du professeur, les jouets des enfants.

target: Il n'y a plus de lait.
tip: 'Ne...plus de' = no more. Like 'ne...pas de', the article disappears after negative + de: Il n'y a plus de pain.

target: Je suis en train de manger.
tip: 'Être en train de + infinitive' = to be in the process of doing. Use to emphasize an ongoing action: Je suis en train de travailler.

target: Est-ce que tu aimes le fromage ?
tip: 'Aimer' + definite article for general likes: 'tu aimes le fromage' (cheese in general). Without article = specific cheese.
'Entrée' here means the entrance. On a menu it's the starter course, never the main dish – English borrowed the word and flipped its meaning.
Flip verb and subject for a polite question: 'Voulez-vous...?' = do you want. The hyphen links them – vous voulez becomes voulez-vous.
Possessive adjectives agree with the noun, not the owner: mon père (m.), ma mère (f.), mes parents (pl.).
'Son/sa/ses' = his/her/its. The form matches the following noun's gender, not the possessor: son mari (her husband, m.).
'Au' = à + le (contraction). 'Aux' = à + les. Mandatory: je vais au cinéma, je parle aux enfants. No contraction with la or l'.
'Souvenir' means a memory first, a keepsake second – both from the verb se souvenir (to remember). So 'des souvenirs' can be either.
Nationality adjectives ending in -ien change to -ienne in feminine: italien → italienne, canadien → canadienne.
'Des' is the plural indefinite article: des frites = some fries. It's required in French where English often uses nothing.

english: Since when have you lived here?
tip: 'Depuis quand' = Since when. 'Depuis combien de temps' = For how long. Both use present tense in French (not past).

english: He eats a lot of vegetables.
tip: After expressions of quantity (beaucoup de, peu de, trop de, assez de), always use 'de' without article: beaucoup de pain (not du pain).

english: Do you have any time left?
tip: 'Rester' can be impersonal: 'il me reste du temps' = I have time left. Reversed construction.

target: J'achète du fromage et de la confiture.
english: I buy some cheese and some jam.
tip: 'Du fromage' (some cheese) and 'de la confiture' (some jam) – partitive articles show an unspecified amount.

target: Quelqu'un a laissé la fenêtre ouverte toute la nuit.
english: Someone left the window open all night.
tip: Laisser plus an adjective means to leave something in a state: a laissé la fenêtre ouverte = left the window open. Ouverte agrees with fenêtre.
Adjectives ending in -eux swap to -euse for a woman: courageux becomes courageuse. Same with heureux/heureuse, sérieux/sérieuse.
Il faut isn't 'he must' – it's impersonal, meaning 'it takes' or 'one needs'. Il faut du courage = courage is needed. The 'il' is a dummy, like English 'it rains'.
Beau becomes bel before a vowel: 'un beau pays' but un bel été. Vieux does the same: vieil homme.
After a quantity word, French drops the article: un morceau de gâteau, never 'de la'. Same for un kilo de, une tasse de.
A few adjectives sit before the noun, and you can stack them: 'un joli petit village' puts both joli and petit up front, unlike most French adjectives.
